# OwnStack — LLM / agent on-ramp (llms.txt)
#
# You are reading this BEFORE the OwnStack CLI is installed. This file tells you
# what OwnStack is, how to install the CLI on a fresh machine, and the full
# command reference so you can drive it. Machine-readable manifest: ./llms.json
#
# Quick start an agent can execute on a clean machine:
#   1. curl -fsSL https://ownstack.org/install.sh | bash      # installs the compiled CLI (macOS/Linux, any arch)
#   2. ownstack login                                          # authenticate (browser; paste token)
#   3. ownstack generate --no-interview myapp rails react --app-number=7   # scaffold (no login needed)
#   4. ownstack deploy myapp                                   # deploy to a stack you own
#
# Homebrew (macOS/Linux): brew install ownstack-org/tap/ownstack
# (After install, `ownstack whatami` reprints this reference; `ownstack docs --json` is the manifest.)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# OwnStack CLI

_Heroku-style ergonomics on infrastructure you own._

## What this is

OwnStack is a control plane for deploying apps onto stacks you own.
The CLI scaffolds composable apps, drives local development, and talks
to the control-plane API for deploys, logs, SSH, and more.

Two big ideas:
  - Apps are composed from atomic components (rails, nestjs, react, angular, docs, wordpress).
  - Stacks are infrastructure you own (AWS, GCP, OpenStack, bare metal). One control plane drives many stacks.

Configuration:
  - Global:  ~/.ownstack/config   (OWNSTACK_API_URL, OWNSTACK_API_TOKEN)
  - Project: .ownstack-config     (OWNSTACK_APP_ID or APP_NAME, OWNSTACK_APP_TOKEN)
  - Linked: .ownstack-app         (app id; created by `ownstack remote -a`)


## Install

```
macOS / Linux:
  curl -fsSL https://ownstack.org/install.sh | bash

From a local clone:
  cd /path/to/ownstack/cli && ./install.sh

Verify:
  ownstack --help

```

## Auth

```
Most control-plane and deploy commands need auth.
  ownstack login                       # browser device-code flow
  ownstack login --token YOUR_TOKEN    # direct (from Settings → API token)
Tokens live in ~/.ownstack/config. Override the API URL with OWNSTACK_API_URL.

```

## Commands

### App generation

Scaffold apps locally from atomic components. No control plane required.

#### `generate`

Generate a composable app from atomic components.

Flags:
- `--push` — Push to ownstack Git after generating (requires login).
- `--no-interview` — Skip interactive prompts (fully non-interactive).
- `--app-number=N` — Numeric suffix when multiple apps share one base.

Examples:
```
ownstack generate    # Interactive — prompts for name and components.
ownstack generate myapp    # Named app, interactive component picker.
ownstack generate myapp rails react docs    # Full stack — Rails API + React frontend + docs site.
ownstack generate myapi rails    # Backend only.
ownstack generate myapp nestjs angular    # NestJS + Angular.
ownstack generate --no-interview myapp rails react --app-number=1    # Fully non-interactive.
ownstack generate --push myapp rails react    # Generate and push to ownstack Git.
```

Notes: Available components: rails, nestjs, react, angular, docs, wordpress.

#### `regenerate` (aliases: regen)

Regenerate an existing app from its saved config.

Examples:
```
ownstack regenerate myapp    # Regenerate by app name.
ownstack regen    # Run from inside an app dir to refresh templates.
ownstack regen rails    # Regenerate only the Rails component.
ownstack regen ssl    # Regenerate only SSL certificates.
```

#### `import`

Import an existing Procfile-only app (any language) into OwnStack.

Flags:
- `--name=NAME` — App name (defaults to the target directory's basename).
- `--app-number=N` — Numeric suffix when multiple apps share one base (default 1).
- `--domain-tld=TLD` — Base TLD for the generated local domain (default ownstack.org).

Examples:
```
ownstack import --name=myapp    # Import the current directory (must contain a Procfile).
ownstack import --name=myapp --app-number=7    # Import with an explicit app number.
ownstack import ./path/to/app --name=myapp    # Import a specific directory.
```

Notes: Requires a Procfile in the target directory. Writes a minimal
.ownstack-config (COMPONENTS="buildpack") so the app deploys via
Procfile + buildpack detection, with no component template.

#### `adopt`

Retrofit OwnStack infrastructure onto an already scaffolded app.

Examples:
```
ownstack adopt    # Adopt the app in the current directory.
ownstack adopt ./path/to/app    # Adopt a specific directory.
```

Notes: Requires a .ownstack-config in the target directory (write one manually,
or run 'ownstack import' for a Procfile-only app). For a Rails backend it
copies the OwnStack infra files (Procfile, Dockerfile, docker-compose.yml,
nginx.conf, config files, the lib/ownstack engine), writes
docker-compose.override.yml and .env, rewrites the docker-compose project
and network names plus the nginx cert paths and redirect ports, generates
a manifest, and sets up cert directories. For an Angular frontend it fixes
the dev-server port. Existing files are skipped (never overwritten). Local
only (no control plane).

#### `list`

List available components.

Examples:
```
ownstack list
```

#### `info`

Show details about a component.

Examples:
```
ownstack info rails
ownstack info react
```

#### `set-app-number`

Set APP_NUMBER for the current app and recompute its local ports.

Examples:
```
ownstack set-app-number 30    # Set app number to 30 (base port 30000, Rails/NestJS 30443, React 30001, Angular 30200).
ownstack set-app-number 1    # Reset to app number 1.
```

Notes: Run from inside an app directory (one containing .ownstack-config). N must be 1 to 99.
Rewrites APP_NUMBER and recomputes the component ports (Rails, NestJS, React, Angular, WordPress)
and API_URL from N. Only ports already present in the config are updated (none are added).
Local only (no control plane). Run `ownstack regen` afterward to apply Redis DB and template changes.

### Local development

Run apps locally with Docker Compose or directly. Most commands run from inside the app directory.

#### `local start` (aliases: local stop, local restart, local down)

Start, stop, restart, or tear down local services.

Flags:
- `-d` — Detached mode.
- `--build` — Rebuild images before starting.

Examples:
```
ownstack local start    # Start backend in foreground.
ownstack local start -d    # Detached.
ownstack local start --build    # Rebuild then start.
ownstack local start rails    # Start a specific service.
ownstack local restart
ownstack local stop
ownstack local down    # Stop and remove containers.
```

#### `local open`

Open the local app URL in a browser.

Examples:
```
ownstack local open
ownstack local open frontend
```

#### `local run`

Run a command inside a local service container.

Examples:
```
ownstack local run rails db:migrate
ownstack local run rails console
ownstack local run rails db:seed
```

#### `local stack`

Manage a local Dokku stack (Docker container) for dev/testing.

Examples:
```
ownstack local stack    # Show status.
ownstack local stack start
ownstack local stack start --no-build
ownstack local stack stop    # Stop and remove.
```

#### `status`

Workspace-wide overview of every local app (ports, infra, issues).

Flags:
- `--json` — Machine-readable JSON instead of the table.

Examples:
```
ownstack status    # Table of all apps found in the workspace apps directory.
ownstack status --json    # JSON output for scripts and agents.
ownstack status /path/to/apps    # Scan an explicit apps directory.
```

Notes: Local only, makes no control-plane request. Scans */.ownstack-config,
auto-detecting the apps directory ($HOME/dev/ownstack/apps, the parent
directory, then the current directory) unless one is passed. Flags
infra gaps (missing Procfile/Dockerfile/etc.), non-standard ports
(Rails = N*1000+443, frontend = N*1000+200), and port collisions.
Exits 1 if no apps directory can be found.

#### `connect`

Open the control plane web UI to link a local app.

Flags:
- `--dev` — Use the local control plane URL.

Examples:
```
ownstack connect
ownstack connect --dev
```

### Control-plane commands

Talk to the control-plane API. Most require `ownstack login` first.

#### `backups`

Fleet-wide backup coverage, every stack and database-bearing app with its schedule and last completed backup.

Flags:
- `--json` — Emit the raw /api/backups/overview response for agents and scripts.

Examples:
```
ownstack backups    # Show fleet-wide backup coverage with NEVER-backed-up apps called out.
```

#### `fleet`

Fleet-wide health in one call, what needs attention (alerts, stuck deploys) plus every app's deploy status.

Flags:
- `--json` — Emit the raw /api/fleet JSON response verbatim (for agents and scripts).

Examples:
```
ownstack fleet    # Human/agent text, attention first then the app roster.
ownstack fleet --json    # Raw JSON for piping into jq or an agent.
```

#### `spend list`

List cloud spend budgets with current cost, limit, and credential.

Examples:
```
ownstack spend list    # Show all cloud budgets (the default subcommand for `ownstack spend`).
```

#### `spend show`

Show the full JSON for one spend budget.

Examples:
```
ownstack spend show 7
```

#### `spend credentials`

List stored stack credentials (id, provider, name, masked summary).

Examples:
```
ownstack spend credentials
ownstack spend credentials show 3    # Reveal the stored credential values for one credential id.
```

#### `spend create`

Create a cloud spend budget tied to a stored credential.

Flags:
- `--name=NAME` — Budget name (required).
- `--credential-id=ID` — Stored stack-credential id to meter against (required, see `ownstack spend credentials`).
- `--limit=USD` — Spend cap in US dollars (required, converted to cents).
- `--alert=PCT` — Alert threshold as a percent of the limit (default 80).

Examples:
```
ownstack spend create --name=prod-aws --credential-id=5 --limit=500 --alert=90
```

#### `spend update`

Update a spend budget's name, limit, or alert threshold.

Flags:
- `--name=NAME` — New budget name.
- `--limit=USD` — New spend cap in US dollars.
- `--alert=PCT` — New alert threshold percent.

Examples:
```
ownstack spend update 7 --name=renamed --limit=250
```

Notes: At least one of --name, --limit, or --alert is required.

#### `spend delete`

Delete a cloud spend budget.

Examples:
```
ownstack spend delete 7
```

#### `credits`

Show your account's usage-credit balance and recent credit activity.

Flags:
- `--json` — Emit the raw /api/pricing/credits response (credits_balance, usd_balance, recent_ledger).

Examples:
```
ownstack credits    # Show balance and recent activity.
ownstack credits --json    # Raw JSON for scripts and agents.
```

#### `credits add`

Buy usage credits for any amount from $1 to $50,000 and get a checkout link.

Flags:
- `--open` — Also open the checkout URL in your browser.
- `--json` — Emit the raw topup response (hosted_url, checkout_id, credit_entry_id, amount_cents).

Examples:
```
ownstack credits add 25    # Start a $25 checkout (12,500,000 credits) and print the payment link.
ownstack credits add 19.99 --open    # Start a $19.99 checkout and open it in the browser.
```

#### `autobuild holds`

List pushes that autobuild held instead of building (supply-chain push watch).

Flags:
- `--all` — Include released and dismissed holds (history), not only open ones.
- `--json` — Emit the raw /api/autobuild_holds response.

Examples:
```
ownstack autobuild holds    # Show what is held right now.
ownstack autobuild holds --all --json    # Full history for scripts and agents.
```

#### `autobuild release`

Build a held push on every app it was holding.

Flags:
- `--json` — Emit the raw response (the resolved hold plus deployments_triggered).

Examples:
```
ownstack autobuild release 7 716d8b34
```

#### `autobuild dismiss`

Clear a held push without building anything.

Flags:
- `--json` — Emit the raw response (the resolved hold).

Examples:
```
ownstack autobuild dismiss 7
```

#### `autobuild rules`

List, add, enable or disable the pre-build diff screen's rules (superuser).

Flags:
- `--json` — Emit the raw rules list.
- `--line=RE` — For added_line rules, the pattern an added line must match.
- `--path=RE` — Only files whose path matches (default any).
- `--exclude=RE` — Skip files whose path matches (generated files, lockfiles).
- `--kind=KIND` — added_line (default), disguised_asset, changed_file, package_scripts or package_dependency_source.

Examples:
```
ownstack autobuild rules
ownstack autobuild rules add eth_rpc_lookup --description="Reads a C2 address from a public Ethereum RPC" --line='eth\.drpc\.org|1rpc\.io'
ownstack autobuild rules disable very_long_source_line
```

#### `remote`

Show or set the control-plane app linked to this repo, or run one remote command against any app.

Flags:
- `-a APP` — With nothing after it, link this repo to the app (by name or id). With a command after it (restart, logs, deploy-log), run that command against the app without linking or writing anything.
- `--relink` — Replace an existing link in this directory (overwrites .ownstack-app / .ownstack-config).
- `--yes` — Link even though the current directory is not a git repository (otherwise you are asked, and a non-interactive run refuses).

Examples:
```
ownstack remote    # Show the currently linked app.
ownstack remote -a my-app    # Link this repo to an app.
ownstack remote -a my-app --relink    # Re-link a directory that already points to a different app.
ownstack remote -a my-app restart worker    # Restart only my-app's worker processes, from any directory. Nothing is linked or written.
ownstack remote -a my-app logs --tail 50    # Recent logs for my-app without linking this directory.
```

Notes: Linking creates `.ownstack-app`, stores your token in `.ownstack-config`, and makes that
token the app's deploy token on the control plane. Outside a git work tree it asks
first, and a non-interactive run refuses unless you pass `--yes`. (The check is "inside
some git work tree", so a subfolder of an unrelated repo still links without asking.)
`remote -a APP <command>` never links: it runs restart, logs or deploy-log against APP
for that one call. Other remote subcommands (stop, start, status, shell, run, open) use
this repo's Dokku git remote and do not take -a.
If the directory is already linked to a *different* app, linking is refused so you
don't clobber another app's link by standing in the wrong repo (a common footgun with
`ownstack app create`, which auto-links the current directory). Pass `--relink` to
override, or `cd` to the intended app's directory first. Re-linking to the same app is
always allowed (it just refreshes the deploy token).

#### `remote restart`

Restart the linked app (or one process type) on its stack(s) via the control plane.

Flags:
- `--app=NAME` — Target app explicitly (defaults to the linked app). Same as `remote -a NAME restart`.
- `--stack=NAME_OR_ID` — Restart on one stack only (defaults to every stack the app is on).

Examples:
```
ownstack remote restart
ownstack remote restart worker    # Restart only the worker processes.
ownstack remote -a myapp restart worker --stack=prod    # Restart another app's worker without linking this folder.
ownstack remote restart --app=myapp --stack=prod
```

Notes: Usage: `ownstack remote restart [TYPE]`. With TYPE (e.g. worker), only that process type restarts (`dokku ps:restart APP TYPE`). If the control
plane does not confirm a single-type restart (an older server restarts everything), the
command warns and exits 1 rather than claim it restarted only TYPE.
Without TYPE it halts and restarts running processes (web + workers). This is what applies config
vars written with `ownstack config:push --no-restart`, since Dokku config:set runs
with --no-restart and leaves running containers on their old environment.
Equivalent to `ownstack app restart <APP>`.

#### `remote logs`

Fetch app logs via the control plane (no SSH needed).

Flags:
- `--tail N` — Last N lines (default 100).
- `--app=NAME` — Target app explicitly (defaults to the linked app). Same as `remote -a NAME logs`.

Examples:
```
ownstack remote logs
ownstack remote logs --tail 200
ownstack remote -a myapp logs --tail 50
OWNSTACK_LOGS_FOLLOW=1 ownstack remote logs    # Stream.
```

#### `remote deploy-log`

View deployment (build + release) logs — same as the UI's "View log".

Flags:
- `--app=NAME` — Target app explicitly.
- `--deployment=ID` — Specific deployment id.

Examples:
```
ownstack remote deploy-log
ownstack remote deploy-log --app=my-app
ownstack remote deploy-log --deployment=123
```

### Signup invitations

Superuser commands for signup-access invitations, mirroring the
/admin/signup-access web UI. An invitation is a one-time access key
that lets someone sign up (for a new account) or join an existing
account. Give it an email and the invitee is emailed the signup link;
omit the email to get a raw token you share yourself.

#### `invites list`

List invitations, most recent first.

Flags:
- `--json` — Emit raw API JSON instead of the formatted table.

Examples:
```
ownstack invites list    # Show id, kind, status, account, email lock, and created date.
```

#### `invites create`

Create an invitation and print the one-time access key.

Flags:
- `--account NAME|SLUG|ID` — Existing account to join (implies --kind join_account).
- `--email ADDR` — Restrict redemption to this address and email them the signup link.
- `--note TEXT` — Internal note shown in the list.
- `--kind new_account|join_account` — Override the kind (default join_account if --account is given, else new_account).
- `--json` — Emit raw API JSON instead of formatted output.

Examples:
```
ownstack invites create --email new@example.com    # New-account invite, emailed to the invitee.
ownstack invites create --account acme --email teammate@acme.com    # Invite someone to join the acme account.
ownstack invites create    # Raw new-account token you share out of band (no email).
```

#### `invites revoke`

Revoke a pending invitation.

Examples:
```
ownstack invites revoke 42    # Revoke invitation id 42.
```

### Deployment

Push code through the control plane. The control plane clones your repo and pushes to Dokku on the stack.

#### `deploy`

Trigger a git-based deploy via the control plane.

Flags:
- `--wait` — Stream deployment output until complete. If a deploy is already in progress, attaches to it instead of erroring.
- `--stack=NAME` — Target a specific stack (for multi-stack apps).
- `--image` — Deploy from a local Docker image instead of git.
- `--clear-stuck` — Clear stuck deployments before deploying.
- `-h, --help` — Print usage and deploy nothing. Any other unknown flag, or a second app argument, is an error (exit 2) and deploys nothing.

Examples:
```
ownstack deploy    # Deploy the linked app.
ownstack deploy my-app    # Deploy by name.
ownstack deploy --wait
ownstack deploy --stack=prod
ownstack deploy --image
ownstack deploy --image myapp:latest
ownstack deploy --clear-stuck
```

Notes: `--wait` attaches to an in-progress deploy rather than failing with "a deploy is
already in progress", so re-running `deploy --wait` always ends up streaming the live
deployment. Use `deploy:status` for a one-shot, non-interactive status read.

#### `deploy:verify`

Check what each stack is actually running against what the control plane recorded as deployed.

Flags:
- `--stack=ID` — Only this stack.
- `--json` — Emit the raw response.

Examples:
```
ownstack deploy:verify
ownstack deploy:verify billing-api --json
```

#### `deploy:status`

Print the latest deployment status per stack (non-interactive; for agents/CI).

Flags:
- `--stack=NAME` — Only show the given stack.
- `--json` — Emit the latest-per-stack deployments as JSON.

Examples:
```
ownstack deploy:status    # Latest status per stack for the linked app.
ownstack deploy:status my-app
ownstack deploy:status --stack=prod --json
```

Notes: Reads /api/apps/:id/deployments so you do not have to scrape `ownstack app info`.
Exit code reflects the most recent deployment: 0 deployed/idle, 1 failed, 2 in-progress.

#### `preflight`

Run local pre-deploy checks to catch common Dokku issues before you push. Also runs as check.

Flags:
- `--dir=PATH` — Check the app in PATH instead of the current directory.
- `--verbose` — Print extra detail (e.g. the matched Procfile web line).

Examples:
```
ownstack preflight    # Check the app in the current directory.
ownstack check    # Same command (check is an alias for preflight).
ownstack preflight --dir=backend
ownstack preflight --verbose
```

Notes: Fully local, makes no control-plane API call. Checks: a Procfile with a web
process, that the web process listens on $PORT (not a hardcoded port), that a
Dockerfile does not hardcode EXPOSE, that a node server package is in
dependencies (not devDependencies), that a buildpack is detectable (Gemfile.lock
for Ruby, a lockfile for Node, or a Dockerfile), that the git working tree is
clean, and that the directory is linked to the control plane (.ownstack-config).
Exit code is 1 when any check fails, 0 otherwise (warnings do not fail).

#### `run`

Run a one-off command in the app's container via the control plane (like heroku run).

Flags:
- `--app=NAME` — Target app (otherwise the first argument, or the linked repo).
- `--stack=NAME` — Run on a specific stack (for multi-stack apps).
- `--no-stream` — Use the buffered endpoint instead of streaming (returns all output at the end).

Examples:
```
ownstack run -- rails db:migrate    # Run in the linked app.
ownstack run myapp -- rails runner 'puts User.count'
ownstack run --app=myapp --stack=prod -- rails db:migrate:status
ownstack run myapp --no-stream -- echo hi
```

Notes: The control plane SSHes to the stack with its stored key, so no local SSH access is
needed (unlike `ownstack remote run`, which shells out from your machine). Output streams
live by default so long tasks (e.g. a data backfill) do not hit the proxy timeout; the
command's remote exit code becomes the exit code of `ownstack run`. Use `--` before the
command so its own flags are not parsed by ownstack. App resolution: `--app`, else the
linked repo, else the first positional argument.

#### `git push`

Push current directory to OwnStack Git (Gitea). Creates repo, optionally links to an app.

Flags:
- `--name=REPO` — New repo name.
- `--app=NAME` — Link the new repo to an existing app.

Examples:
```
ownstack git push    # From a linked app dir.
ownstack git push --name=my-app
ownstack git push --app=my-app
```

### Stack management

Operations on stack infrastructure — plugins, data, backups, patches, maintenance.

#### `stack create`

Provision a new managed stack (AWS, GCP, Azure, OpenStack, DigitalOcean, Hetzner, or SSH-managed). Mirrors the dashboard "New Stack" form.

Flags:
- `--provider=aws|gcp|azure|openstack|digitalocean|hetzner|ssh` — Cloud provider (required).
- `--credential=NAME_OR_ID` — Stored stack credential (required for managed providers). Resolves by name via /api/stack_credentials.
- `--region=NAME` — Cloud region (required for aws/azure/openstack/digitalocean/hetzner; e.g. DigitalOcean nyc3, Hetzner ash, hil, fsn1).
- `--gcp-project=PROJECT_ID` — GCP project to deploy into.
- `--ram=GB` — Desired RAM in GiB (2..128).
- `--disk=GB` — Root disk in GB (10..1000).
- `--ssh-host=HOST` — For provider=ssh; remote SSH host.
- `--ssh-port=PORT` — For provider=ssh; SSH port (default 22).
- `--ssh-username=USER` — For provider=ssh; SSH username.
- `--ssh-private-key=PATH` — For provider=ssh; path to a private-key file.
- `--ssh-password=PASS` — For provider=ssh; password (use instead of --ssh-private-key).

Examples:
```
ownstack stack create stage-gcp --provider=gcp --credential='Google Cloud' --gcp-project=my-gcp-proj --ram=64 --disk=200    # GCP n2-highmem-8 sized stack (8 vCPU, 64 GiB).
ownstack stack create stage-east --provider=aws --credential='AWS prod' --region=us-west-2 --ram=64 --disk=200    # AWS r6i.2xlarge sized stack.
ownstack stack create do-test --provider=digitalocean --credential='DigitalOcean' --region=nyc3 --ram=2    # DigitalOcean droplet (s-1vcpu-2gb) for OSS-app dogfooding.
ownstack stack create my-hetzner-box --provider=hetzner --credential='Hetzner' --region=ash --ram=8    # Hetzner stack in Ashburn, US. Server type is picked live (cheapest current x86 type meeting the RAM ask in that location); the cheap CX line is EU-only (fsn1/nbg1/hel1), US locations carry CPX.
ownstack stack create my-server --provider=ssh --ssh-host=1.2.3.4 --ssh-username=ubuntu --ssh-private-key=~/.ssh/id_ed25519    # Adopt an existing host you SSH into.
```

#### `stack destroy`

Tear down a stack and deprovision its cloud resources. Symmetric with `stack create`. Interactive confirmation by default; use `--yes` for scripts. Without `--yes` you must type the stack name; if the CLI cannot load the stack to learn its name, it refuses and destroys nothing.

Flags:
- `--yes, -y` — Skip the interactive confirmation prompt (required for non-interactive callers).

Examples:
```
ownstack stack destroy stage-gcp    # Interactive — prompts you to retype the stack name.
ownstack stack destroy 50 --yes    # Non-interactive, by id.
```

#### `stack retry`

Retry provisioning for a stack stuck in pending, provisioning, or failed. Calls `POST /api/stacks/:id/retry_provisioning`, which resets the status to pending, clears the provisioning error, and re-triggers provisioning. Non-destructive (keeps the stack record, id, and config); use this instead of destroy + create when a provision failed transiently.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack retry prod-hub    # Re-trigger provisioning for a stack whose provision failed, by name.
ownstack stack retry 56    # Retry by id.
```

#### `stack unmanaged`

List orphan cloud instances — instances that exist under the account's AWS/GCP credentials but are tracked by no managed stack (e.g. left behind by a deleted stack or a crashed provision, still billing). CLI parity with the web Stacks page and `GET /api/stacks/unmanaged`. GCP credentials with no associated stack have no derivable project and are reported as a scan notice rather than scanned.

Flags:
- `--json` — Emit the raw API payload (count, instances, errors, scanned, timed_out) instead of the table.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack unmanaged    # List orphan instances for the current profile's account.
OWNSTACK_PROFILE=ownstack ownstack stack unmanaged --json    # Raw JSON for a specific account, e.g. for scripting.
```

#### `stack unmanaged destroy`

Terminate an orphan instance by its instance id. Looks the instance up in the live scan to find the provider-specific parameters, then calls `DELETE /api/stacks/unmanaged`, which refuses anything that backs a managed stack. Not reversible. Interactive confirmation by default.

Flags:
- `--yes, -y` — Skip the confirmation prompt (required for non-interactive callers).

Examples:
```
ownstack stack unmanaged destroy i-06ba7d4af55693aa7    # Interactive — prompts before terminating the cloud instance.
ownstack stack unmanaged destroy i-080eb746afdaa1022 --yes    # Non-interactive teardown of a known orphan.
```

#### `stack containers`

List docker containers on a stack with state classification (running, exited, unhealthy, orphan, stale). Stale containers are running but not in their app's current ps:scale — the usual cause of "missing" memory after repeated ps:rebuild or OOM-restart cycles.

Flags:
- `--app=NAME` — Only list containers belonging to this Dokku app.
- `--state=running|exited|unhealthy|orphan|stale` — Filter to one state. Stale = running but outside ps:scale.
- `--json` — Emit raw JSON instead of the table view.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack containers <STACK>    # All containers across all apps on the stack.
ownstack stack containers <STACK> --app=<APP> --state=stale    # Just the stale Sidekiq survivors for one app.
```

#### `stack reconcile-ps`

Reap containers not in `dokku ps:scale`. Use this to clean up OOM-restart survivors that Dokku stopped tracking. Default is live reap; use --dry-run to preview.

Flags:
- `--stack=NAME` — Target stack (otherwise uses the linked app's stack).
- `--dry-run` — Identify what would be removed without invoking `docker rm`.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack reconcile-ps <APP> --stack=<STACK> --dry-run    # Preview the reap.
ownstack stack reconcile-ps <APP> --stack=<STACK>    # Actually reap.
```

#### `stack resize-disk`

Grow the stack's root volume. AWS extends the volume online (instance stays up); OpenStack stops the server, extends, then restarts.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack resize-disk staging-hub 500    # Grow staging-hub's root volume to 500 GB (AWS, online).
```

Notes: New size must be greater than the current size and between 10 and 1000 GB.
The filesystem is grown automatically after the volume extends. Watch
progress with `ownstack stack disk-usage <STACK>`.

#### `stack resize-ram`

Change the instance RAM. Stops and restarts the instance to apply the new machine type.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack resize-ram <STACK> 16    # Resize to 16 GB RAM (causes a restart).
```

Notes: Supported sizes (GB): 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. The instance is stopped,
resized, and restarted, so expect brief downtime.

#### `stack add-local`

Create a local stack (dev only).

Examples:
```
ownstack stack add-local [NAME]
```

#### `stack plugin-install`

Install a Dokku plugin on a stack.

Flags:
- `--stack=NAME` — Target stack (otherwise prompts/uses default).

Examples:
```
ownstack stack plugin-install letsencrypt
ownstack stack plugin-install --stack=prod letsencrypt
```

#### `stack data`

List databases and manage volumes on a stack.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack data databases <STACK>
ownstack stack data volumes <STACK>
ownstack stack data volumes <STACK> add <app> <host_path> <container_path>    # Mount a host directory into the container so writes survive a redeploy. Convention: /var/lib/dokku/data/storage/<app> on the host. Restart the app to pick it up.
ownstack stack data volumes <STACK> remove <app> <mount_spec>    # mount_spec is host_path:container_path, as printed by the list form.
```

Notes: The control plane services these over SSH to the box, so they can take
30-60s on a busy stack. That is normal, not a hang.

A volume is how an app keeps data across deploys. Without one, anything
the container writes to disk is discarded when it is rebuilt.

#### `stack backup`

Run, list, enable, and inspect stack backups.

Flags:
- `--mode=application|native|both` — For `enable`. application = per-database dumps (restorable via `app data restore`); native = provider disk snapshot + AMI (whole-server restore); both = one nightly job produces both. Default native.
- `--cron=EXPR` — For `enable`. Schedule, default 0 3 * * *.
- `--retention=N` — For `enable`. Completed backups to keep, default 7.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack backup run <STACK>
ownstack stack backup list <STACK>    # Lists job id, status, type, and timestamp. Use the job id with `app data restore --backup=ID`.
ownstack stack backup enable <STACK> --mode=both    # Nightly disk snapshot AND database dumps in one job.
ownstack stack backup config <STACK>
```

#### `app data restore`

Restore an app's database from a stack backup job (dokku postgres:import / mysql:import).

Flags:
- `--backup=JOB_ID` — Stack backup job id (required, from `stack backup list`).
- `--stack=NAME` — Stack the backup lives on. Defaults to the app's stack.
- `--source-service=SVC` — Service dump inside the backup to import. Enables cross-app restores, e.g. restore postgres-myapp into postgres-myapp-staging. Without it, only an exact match on the app's own linked service is accepted; on mismatch the error lists available services.
- `--source=s3|host` — Where to read the dump from. Default prefers the on-host dump and falls back to S3 if the host file is gone. Pass s3 to restore from the object-storage copy (works cross-stack, e.g. restore prod's S3 dump onto staging); host to force the on-host file.

Examples:
```
ownstack app data restore my-app --backup=42    # Restore the app's own dump from backup job 42.
ownstack app data restore my-app-staging --backup=42 --source-service=postgres-my-app    # Seed staging from the production dump in the same backup.
ownstack app data restore my-app-staging --backup=42 --source-service=postgres-my-app --source=s3    # Stream the production dump straight from S3 into staging (no host copy needed).
```

#### `stack patches`

List or apply stack patches (severity, deadlines, auto-on-deploy).

Examples:
```
ownstack stack patches <STACK>    # Show patches with status, severity, overdue, and auto-on-deploy flags.
ownstack stack patches apply <STACK>    # Apply all pending patches now (or wait for the next deploy if they're auto-apply).
ownstack stack patches overdue    # Fleet view, stacks with overdue mandatory patches.
ownstack stack patches overdue --json    # Same, JSON output (pipe to jq for scripting).
```

#### `stack disk-usage`

Show disk usage on a stack (via SSH).

Examples:
```
ownstack stack disk-usage <STACK>
```

#### `stack info`

Host/container facts read live over SSH (cores, RAM, container memory limit, disk type).

Flags:
- `--json` — Emit the facts as JSON.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack info <STACK>
ownstack stack info <STACK> --json
```

Notes: Surfaces CPU cores, total host RAM, the container memory limit (cgroup; "unlimited" means
bounded by host RAM), and whether the root disk is SSD or rotational, plus the provisioned
sizes. Makes correct DB/app tuning a read instead of an SSH expedition (free -h,
/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max, lsblk -d -o NAME,ROTA by hand).

#### `stack health`

Heartbeat health for a stack, off-box reachability plus on-box agent, provider state, and active alerts.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack health <STACK>
```

#### `stack memory`

Host memory + per-container breakdown from the on-box heartbeat agent.

Flags:
- `--json` — Emit the latest_snapshot + recent_memory shape as JSON.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack memory <STACK>
ownstack stack memory <STACK> --json
```

#### `stack resources`

Memory budget — per-app limits vs usable host RAM, with over-allocation and uncapped-app warnings.

Flags:
- `--json` — Emit the full resource_budget payload as JSON.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack resources <STACK>
ownstack stack resources <STACK> --json
```

#### `stack reboot`

Graceful reboot of the stack's host VM via the provider SDK.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack reboot <STACK>
```

#### `stack start`

Power on a stopped host.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack start <STACK>
```

#### `stack stop`

Power off the host (volumes persist).

Examples:
```
ownstack stack stop <STACK>
```

#### `stack host-actions`

Recent host start/stop/reboot history (last 25 entries).

Examples:
```
ownstack stack host-actions <STACK>
```

#### `stack add-key`

Add your local SSH public key to the stack for direct ssh access.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack add-key <STACK>    # Auto-detect a local public key and register it.
ownstack stack add-key <STACK> --key=~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub    # Register a specific public key file.
```

#### `stack ownstackd`

Manage the on-stack ownstackd daemon (replaces SSH-from-control-plane for routine ops).

Examples:
```
ownstack stack ownstackd status <STACK>    # Show enabled / alive / last-seen / version.
ownstack stack ownstackd enable <STACK>    # Generate a stack-scoped token, flip the flag, print install one-liner.
ownstack stack ownstackd disable <STACK>    # Flip the flag off. Token kept so re-enable is one command. Daemon idles.
ownstack stack ownstackd rotate <STACK>    # Invalidate the existing token and issue a new one. Reinstall daemon with the new token.
```

#### `stack add-ons`

List, add, and remove a stack's add-ons (Heartbeat, Private Network).

Flags:
- `--json` — Emit the add-on list as JSON.
- `--auth-key=KEY` — Tailscale auth key (tskey-auth-...) or Headscale pre-auth key. Prompted for (hidden) when omitted, which keeps it out of shell history.
- `--login-server=URL` — https URL of your Headscale server. Omit for Tailscale.
- `--yes` — Skip the confirmation on remove.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack add-ons <STACK>    # Show each add-on as added / joining / failed / available, with the tailnet IP once joined.
ownstack stack add-ons add <STACK> tailscale    # Join the stack to your tailnet (prompts for the auth key).
ownstack stack add-ons add <STACK> tailscale --login-server=https://hs.example.com    # Join your own Headscale instead of Tailscale.
ownstack stack add-ons remove <STACK> tailscale --yes    # Log the host out of the tailnet and stop tailscaled (also cleans up after a failed join).
```

#### `stack maintenance`

Prune images, schedule jobs, forecast disk, scan CVEs.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack maintenance prune-images <STACK>
ownstack stack maintenance prune-build-cache <STACK>
ownstack stack maintenance schedules <STACK>
ownstack stack maintenance schedule add <STACK> --action=prune_images --cadence=weekly
ownstack stack maintenance forecast <STACK>    # Days until 80% / 90% full.
ownstack stack maintenance cve <STACK>    # Trivy scan of dokku/* images.
```

#### `stack share`

Share a stack with another OwnStack account by email.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack share <STACK> <EMAIL>    # Invite an account by email. Shows as pending until accepted.
ownstack stack shares <STACK>    # List shares with status (pending / accepted) and who accepted.
ownstack stack unshare <STACK> <EMAIL>    # Revoke a share. The account immediately loses access.
ownstack stack share-accept <STACK>    # Accept a stack shared with your account (recipient side).
ownstack stack share-reject <STACK>    # Reject a pending invitation (recipient side).
ownstack stack leave <STACK>    # Leave a stack that was shared with you. Apps your account deployed keep running.
```

#### `stack subscriptions (owner)`

See the managed stacks sold on a host you own.

Examples:
```
ownstack stack subscriptions <STACK>    # Reservation ledger, one row per buyer, with $/mo.
```

### Managed stacks (pay-to-play shared hosting)

A managed stack is $5/mo per unit on a shared host that accepts tenants.
One unit reserves 4GB RAM and 10 app slots; two units equal a whole
4vCPU/8GB box. You deploy apps onto it within that quota like any stack,
and nothing else: no host operations, no access to other tenants' apps.
Buying starts an OwnBilling subscription; cancel any time.

#### `managed-stacks`

List your managed stacks, browse the catalog, buy and cancel.

Examples:
```
ownstack managed-stacks    # Your managed stacks across all hosts, with app usage and price.
ownstack managed-stacks catalog    # Hosts selling managed stacks, with live remaining capacity.
ownstack managed-stacks buy <STACK> --units 2    # Buy two units (8GB reserved, 20 app slots, $10/mo).
ownstack managed-stacks cancel <MANAGED_STACK_ID>    # Cancel your managed stack. Refuses while apps remain unless --force.
```

### Clusters and load balancing

A cluster pools stacks behind a hostname. It owns a Caddy proxy app (deployed to N proxy stacks
for redundancy) and routes traffic to member app-stacks. Pick the edge mode at create time:
  - dns_rr      DNS round-robin. Free, works anywhere.
  - cloudflare  Proxied origins, sub-second failover.
  - aws_alb     AWS ALB (LBaaS).

The proxy app is just an OwnStack app — same logs / restart / SSH / scale / maintenance as
anything else. The cluster regenerates its Caddyfile on member changes and dokku-deploys it.

#### `cluster list`

List clusters in the active profile.

Examples:
```
ownstack cluster list
```

#### `cluster show`

Show edge / proxies / members / status for a cluster.

Examples:
```
ownstack cluster show <NAME>
```

#### `cluster create`

Create a cluster and stamp its proxy app from the Caddy template.

Flags:
- `--hostname=HOST` — Public hostname.
- `--edge=MODE` — dns_rr | cloudflare | aws_alb.
- `--proxy-count=N` — Number of proxy replicas.

Examples:
```
ownstack cluster create <NAME> --hostname=api.example.com \
  --edge=dns_rr --proxy-count=2
```

#### `cluster destroy`

Destroy a cluster (proxy app stays unless --with-proxy). Asks you to confirm by typing the name or id, unless you pass `--yes`.

Flags:
- `--with-proxy` — Also destroy the proxy app.
- `--yes, -y` — Skip the confirmation prompt (you otherwise type the name or id back). Required for scripts and non-interactive callers.

Examples:
```
ownstack cluster destroy <NAME>
```

#### `cluster member`

Add, drain, undrain, remove, or reweight member apps.

Examples:
```
ownstack cluster member add <CLUSTER> <APP>
ownstack cluster member drain <CLUSTER> <APP>    # Existing connections finish, no new ones.
ownstack cluster member undrain <CLUSTER> <APP>
ownstack cluster member remove <CLUSTER> <APP>
ownstack cluster member weight <CLUSTER> <APP> <0-1000>    # Set the member's load-balancer weight. 0 = no traffic (true drain); used for blue/green flips.
```

#### `cluster deploy`

Deploy across cluster members.

Flags:
- `--strategy=MODE` — parallel (default) | rolling. Rolling drains then deploys one at a time.

Examples:
```
ownstack cluster deploy <CLUSTER>
ownstack cluster deploy <CLUSTER> --strategy=rolling
```

#### `cluster autodeploy`

Show or toggle cluster autodeploy. When enabled, a push to the cluster's repo fires a zero-downtime rolling release across members (drain, deploy, health-gate, restore) instead of deploying any single member in place. The Heroku "automatic deploys" analog, made safe for a self-hosted cluster.

Flags:
- `--branch=REF` — Only auto-deploy pushes to this branch. Omit to accept whatever branch each member app is configured for; pass an empty value to clear the filter.

Examples:
```
ownstack cluster autodeploy <CLUSTER>    # Show the current autodeploy state.
ownstack cluster autodeploy <CLUSTER> on    # Enable rolling autodeploy on push.
ownstack cluster autodeploy <CLUSTER> on --branch=main    # Enable, restricted to the main branch.
ownstack cluster autodeploy <CLUSTER> off    # Disable autodeploy.
```

Notes: Requires the GitHub webhook (autobuild) to be installed on at least
one member app so deliveries arrive. Autodeploy then routes that
delivery to a rolling cluster release rather than an in-place deploy.
A push is ignored while a previous rolling release is still in flight.

#### `cluster status`

Topology view of a cluster (variants, upstreams, live state).

Examples:
```
ownstack cluster status <CLUSTER>
```

#### `cluster domain`

Manage the hostnames a cluster fronts. A cluster can serve many hostnames; cutover happens atomically across all of them.

Examples:
```
ownstack cluster domain list <CLUSTER>
ownstack cluster domain add <CLUSTER> example.com
ownstack cluster domain add <CLUSTER> app.example.com
ownstack cluster domain remove <CLUSTER> app.example.com
```

#### `cluster variant`

Manage named swappable backend groups (e.g. heroku, hetzner). Each variant has weight (0 standby, >0 receives traffic) and status (active or draining).

Flags:
- `--weight=N` — Traffic weight, 0..1000. 0 = standby.
- `--status=STATE` — active | draining (draining stops new connections).
- `--description=TEXT` — Human-readable note.

Examples:
```
ownstack cluster variant list <CLUSTER>
ownstack cluster variant add <CLUSTER> heroku --weight=100
ownstack cluster variant add <CLUSTER> hetzner --weight=0
ownstack cluster variant update <CLUSTER> heroku --weight=0
ownstack cluster variant remove <CLUSTER> staging
```

#### `cluster upstream`

Manage per-variant, per-domain routes. An upstream is either an internal OwnStack app or an external HTTPS URL. Exactly one of --url or --app is required.

Flags:
- `--variant=NAME` — Variant this upstream belongs to.
- `--hostname=HOST` — Restrict to one hostname; omit to serve all hostnames on the cluster.
- `--url=URL` — External upstream (https://...). Use for routing to a Heroku / external backend.
- `--app=APP` — Internal OwnStack app (resolves to its stack IPs).
- `--weight=N` — Upstream weight 0..1000.
- `--host-header=HOST` — Host header to send upstream (defaults to the cluster hostname).

Examples:
```
ownstack cluster upstream list <CLUSTER>
ownstack cluster upstream add <CLUSTER> \
  --variant=heroku --hostname=example.com \
  --url=https://my-app.herokuapp.com
ownstack cluster upstream add <CLUSTER> \
  --variant=hetzner --hostname=example.com \
  --url=https://new.example.com
ownstack cluster upstream remove <CLUSTER> <UPSTREAM_ID>
```

#### `cluster switch`

Atomically flip the active variant; reweights everything inside a transaction and fires one reconcile. All hostnames cutover together.

Flags:
- `--to=NAME` — Name of the variant that should receive 100% of traffic.

Examples:
```
ownstack cluster switch <CLUSTER> --to=hetzner
ownstack cluster switch <CLUSTER> --to=heroku    # Roll back in seconds if the new variant misbehaves.
```

### App management

Operations on apps already in the control plane.

#### `app list` (aliases: apps)

List apps in the active account.

Examples:
```
ownstack app list
ownstack apps
```

#### `app create`

Register an existing repo as an app on a stack (Heroku `apps:create` style), then optionally link the current directory.

Flags:
- `--stack=NAME_OR_ID` — Target stack (required).
- `--git-url=URL` — Git repository URL to deploy from.
- `--git-branch=BRANCH` — Branch to deploy (default main).
- `--subdir=PATH` — Subdirectory to build from in a monorepo.
- `--build-type=buildpacks|dockerfile` — Build strategy (default buildpacks).
- `--app-type=raw|rails|nestjs|angular|dockerfile` — App type preset (default raw).
- `--components=LIST` — Comma-separated component list (default buildpack).
- `--description=TEXT` — Human-readable description.
- `--no-services` — Provision no database, redis, or other services.
- `--postgres` — Provision Postgres (use --no-postgres to disable).
- `--redis` — Provision Redis (use --no-redis to disable).
- `--mysql` — Provision MySQL (use --no-mysql to disable).
- `--mongo` — Provision Mongo (use --no-mongo to disable).
- `--no-link` — Do not link the current directory to the new app.
- `--relink` — Replace an existing link in this directory.

Examples:
```
ownstack app create myapp --stack=prod --git-url=https://github.com/me/myapp.git
ownstack app create myapp --stack=prod --postgres --redis
ownstack app create myapp --stack=prod --no-services --no-link
```

Notes: POSTs /api/apps with the app fields, applies any service flags with a
follow-up PATCH, and (unless --no-link) links the cwd via the
remote-add helper so `ownstack deploy` uses this account. The stack is
resolved by name or numeric id and is required. Service flags are
opt-in; pass --postgres, --redis, --mysql, or --mongo to provision, or
the --no-* form to turn one off. Outside a git work tree the link step
asks first (a non-interactive run skips it; the app is still created),
then link with `ownstack remote -a NAME --yes`. Note that the --template=landing
launch orchestration is bash-only and is not yet supported here.

#### `app update`

Patch fields on an existing app (same flag shape as app create); only the flags you pass are changed.

Flags:
- `--stack=NAME_OR_ID` — Repoint the app's primary stack. app stacks:add only adds an association; this is what moves the stack the app reports as its own. Deploy to the new stack and cut DNS over first, then remove the old association with app stacks:remove.
- `--git-url=URL` — Git repository URL.
- `--git-branch=BRANCH` — Branch to deploy.
- `--subdir=PATH` — Monorepo subdirectory.
- `--build-type=buildpacks|dockerfile` — Build strategy.
- `--app-type=raw|rails|nestjs|angular|dockerfile` — App type preset.
- `--description=TEXT` — Human-readable description.
- `--display-name=TEXT` — Display name shown in the dashboard.
- `--postgres` — Provision Postgres (use --no-postgres to disable).
- `--redis` — Provision Redis (use --no-redis to disable).
- `--mysql` — Provision MySQL (use --no-mysql to disable).
- `--mongo` — Provision Mongo (use --no-mongo to disable).

Examples:
```
ownstack app update myapp --git-branch=release
ownstack app update myapp --postgres --no-redis
ownstack app update myapp --stack=prod-hub    # Make prod-hub the app's primary stack after deploying there.
```

Notes: Resolves the app by name or id, then PATCHes /api/apps/{id} with just
the fields you set. Pass at least one flag. Service flags accept both
the bare form (--postgres) and the --no- form (--no-postgres).

#### `config:list` (aliases: config)

List an app's environment variables as KEY=VALUE lines.

Flags:
- `--app=NAME` — App name. `--app NAME` works too. Defaults to the linked app only when the flag is absent: the flag is never ignored, so it can no longer answer with another app's vars.

Examples:
```
ownstack config:list --app=myapp
ownstack config --app=myapp
```

#### `config:get`

Print the value of one config var (exits 1 if it is not set).

Flags:
- `--app=NAME` — App name. `--app NAME` works too. Defaults to the linked app only when the flag is absent: the flag is never ignored, so it can no longer answer with another app's vars.

Examples:
```
ownstack config:get DATABASE_URL --app=myapp
```

#### `config:set`

Set one or more config vars (KEY=VALUE), stored on the control plane.

Flags:
- `--app=NAME` — App name. `--app NAME` works too. Defaults to the linked app only when the flag is absent: the flag is never ignored, so it can no longer answer with another app's vars.

Examples:
```
ownstack config:set RAILS_ENV=production --app=myapp
ownstack config:set FOO=bar BAZ=qux --app=myapp
```

Notes: Values are stored on the app. They auto-sync only to stacks listed in the
app's auto_sync_stack_ids; otherwise run `ownstack config:push` to apply them
to a running stack (which restarts it).

#### `config:unset`

Remove one or more config vars.

Flags:
- `--app=NAME` — App name. `--app NAME` works too. Defaults to the linked app only when the flag is absent: the flag is never ignored, so it can no longer answer with another app's vars.

Examples:
```
ownstack config:unset FOO --app=myapp
ownstack config:unset FOO BAZ --app=myapp
```

#### `config:push`

Push managed config vars to a deployed stack and restart it so they take effect.

Flags:
- `--app=NAME` — App name. `--app NAME` works too. Defaults to the linked app only when the flag is absent: the flag is never ignored, so it can no longer answer with another app's vars.
- `--stack=NAME_OR_ID` — Target stack (required when the app has more than one stack).
- `--no-restart` — Store the vars without restarting. Running containers keep the previous values until the next restart or deploy.

Examples:
```
ownstack config:push --app=myapp
ownstack config:push --app=myapp --stack=prod
ownstack config:push --app=myapp --stack=prod DATABASE_URL REDIS_URL
ownstack config:push --app=myapp --no-restart
```

Notes: Applies the control-plane config vars to the stack via dokku config:set, then
restarts the app so the running containers pick them up. Pass specific KEYs to
push only those; omit to push all.

The restart is the part that matters. Dokku config:set runs with --no-restart so
the write is instant, which means the vars sit in Dokku's store while every
running container keeps its old environment. Verifying with `ownstack run printenv
MY_VAR` does not catch this: `run` starts a fresh one-off container that reads the
new value regardless. Check `ownstack stack containers <STACK> --app=<APP>` instead
and look at the container age, or trust this command to restart for you.

With --no-restart, apply the vars later with `ownstack remote restart` (or
`ownstack app restart <APP>`) or on your next deploy.

#### `app stacks`

List the stacks an app is deployed to.

#### `app stacks:add`

Assign an app to an additional stack so deploys also target it.

Examples:
```
ownstack app stacks:add <APP> <STACK>
ownstack app stacks:add <STACK>    # Assign the linked app.
```

#### `app stacks:remove`

Unassign an app from a stack so deploys stop targeting it.

Examples:
```
ownstack app stacks <APP>
```

Notes: This drops the control-plane assignment ONLY. It does not tear down the
Dokku app already running on that stack.

To also remove the containers and linked services, nuke FIRST, then
unassign, because nuke resolves the stack through this same assignment:

  ownstack app nuke <APP> --stack=<STACK>
  ownstack app stacks:remove <APP> <STACK>

Doing it in the other order leaves an orphaned Dokku app on the stack
with no control-plane record pointing at it.

#### `app test` (aliases: app tests)

Run the app's test command as a one-off process on its stack (Heroku `heroku run` style) and stream output live.

Flags:
- `--command=CMD` — One-off command to run instead of the configured test_command.
- `--stack=ID` — Run on a specific stack (defaults to the app's primary/deployable stack).
- `--no-wait` — Start the run and return immediately instead of streaming.
- `--json` — Print the created run as JSON (no streaming).

Examples:
```
ownstack app test <APP>    # Run the configured test command and stream output.
ownstack app test <APP> --command="bundle exec rspec spec/models"    # One-off ad-hoc command.
ownstack app test <APP> --stack=43 --no-wait
```

Notes: Runs inside a fresh container booted from the app's deployed image,
so the test sees the real config vars and linked add-ons
(DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, ...). Exit code is captured via a sentinel
since `dokku run` does not forward it. Requires jq for live output.
Exit status: 0 passed, 1 failed, 2 timeout/unknown.

#### `app test:list` (aliases: app tests:list)

List recent test runs (status, exit code, duration, command).

Flags:
- `--json` — Raw JSON array.

Examples:
```
ownstack app test:list <APP>
```

#### `app test:show` (aliases: app tests:show)

Show a test run's details and full output.

Flags:
- `--json` — Raw JSON.

Examples:
```
ownstack app test:show <RUN_ID> <APP>
```

#### `app test:config` (aliases: app tests:config)

Show or set the app's test command.

Flags:
- `--command=CMD` — Set the test command (omit to just show current config).

Examples:
```
ownstack app test:config <APP>
ownstack app test:config <APP> --command="npm test"
```

#### `app destroy` (aliases: app rm, app delete)

Destroy a control-plane app and tear down its Dokku app + linked services on every stack it's deployed to.

Flags:
- `--yes` — Skip the interactive name-match confirmation.

Examples:
```
ownstack app destroy <NAME>    # Interactive — prompts you to retype the name to confirm.
ownstack app destroy my-metabase --yes    # Non-interactive (CI/scripts).
ownstack app rm <UUID>    # Same as destroy, accepts UUID instead of name.
```

Notes: Server-side `AppDestroyWorker` runs the SSH cleanup
(apps:destroy plus postgres/mysql/redis/etc. unlink + destroy).
Persistent volumes are not removed automatically — host
`/var/lib/dokku/data/storage/*` dirs survive for now.

#### `app autodeploy`

Show or toggle per-(app, stack) autodeploy. Turning autodeploy on also installs the GitHub push webhook if it isn't there yet — both layers have to be enabled for pushes to actually deploy.

Flags:
- `--stack=NAME_OR_ID` — Toggle on a single stack instead of every linked stack.

Examples:
```
ownstack app autodeploy <APP>    # Show the per-stack autodeploy state.
ownstack app autodeploy <APP> on    # Turn autodeploy on for every linked stack (and install the webhook if missing).
ownstack app autodeploy <APP> --stack=<STACK> off    # Turn it off for one stack.
```

#### `app autobuild`

Manage the GitHub push webhook on an app's repository. Required for autodeploy to actually fire.

Examples:
```
ownstack app autobuild <APP>    # Show enabled state and the GitHub webhook id.
ownstack app autobuild:enable <APP>    # Install the GitHub push webhook on the app's repo.
ownstack app autobuild:disable <APP>    # Remove the webhook (deploys still work manually).
```

Notes: GitHub autobuild and per-stack autodeploy are two independent layers.
Autobuild owns the webhook on the repo; autodeploy owns whether a
received webhook actually enqueues a deploy. `app autodeploy on` will
enable autobuild for you when both are off, but you can also manage
the webhook directly with these commands.

#### `app autobuild:consolidate`

Collapse redundant per-app GitHub webhooks on the same repo down to a single survivor. Cleans up the per-app era for accounts that ran ahead of the share-on-create fix.

Flags:
- `--dry-run` — Report the plan but don't modify anything.

Examples:
```
ownstack app autobuild:consolidate <APP>    # Consolidate the repo this app belongs to.
ownstack app autobuild:consolidate <APP> --dry-run    # Preview the consolidation before doing it.
```

Notes: Picks the lowest-id app's hook as canonical, deletes every other
GitHub-side hook for the same repo via the deploy-token user's
GitHub credentials, and re-points all sibling apps at the survivor.
--dry-run shows the plan without touching GitHub or the DB.

#### `app cron`

Manage scheduled jobs that run via `dokku run <app> <command>` on the stack's crontab.

Examples:
```
ownstack app cron <APP>    # List scheduled jobs.
ownstack app cron:add <APP> '0 3 * * *' 'rake nightly' --description='nightly DB cleanup'    # Add a nightly job at 03:00.
ownstack app cron:add <APP> '*/15 * * * *' 'curl -fsS http://localhost/health'    # Health check every 15 minutes.
ownstack app cron:update <APP> 12 --schedule='0 4 * * *'    # Change job
ownstack app cron:disable <APP> 12    # Pause a job without deleting it.
ownstack app cron:enable <APP> 12    # Resume a paused job.
ownstack app cron:remove <APP> 12    # Delete a job permanently.
ownstack app cron:sync <APP>    # Force re-push of the managed crontab block to every deployable stack.
```

Notes: The control plane keeps a managed block in the dokku user's crontab,
delimited by `# OWNSTACK-CRON: <dokku-app> BEGIN/END` markers. Any
add/update/remove triggers a re-push to every deployable stack. Use
`cron:sync` to force a re-push without changing the job set (useful
after restoring a stack or recovering from drift).

Schedule is standard 5-field cron (`minute hour day-of-month month
day-of-week`). Commands run inside `dokku run`, so use your app's
process binary directly (`rake db:cleanup`, `python manage.py jobs:run`).
`%` in the command must be escaped as `\%` — cron treats unescaped
`%` as a stdin separator.

#### `app protect`

Gate an app behind HTTP Basic Auth (the dokku-http-auth plugin), with a user list and an IP bypass allow-list.

Flags:
- `--user=NAME` — Username to create (protect:enable, protect:add-user, protect:remove-user).
- `--password=PASS` — Password for the user (protect:enable, protect:add-user).
- `--ip=CIDR` — IP address or CIDR range to allow or disallow (protect:allow-ip, protect:disallow-ip).

Examples:
```
ownstack app protect:status <APP>    # Show auth status, users, and allowed IPs.
ownstack app protect:enable <APP> --user=admin --password=secret    # Enable HTTP Basic Auth with a first user.
ownstack app protect:disable <APP>    # Turn off HTTP Basic Auth.
ownstack app protect:add-user <APP> --user=teammate --password=pw    # Add another user.
ownstack app protect:remove-user <APP> --user=teammate    # Remove a user.
ownstack app protect:allow-ip <APP> --ip=203.0.113.0/24    # Let an IP range bypass the auth prompt.
ownstack app protect:disallow-ip <APP> --ip=203.0.113.0/24    # Remove an IP range from the bypass allow-list.
```

Notes: Protects every request to the app with a username/password prompt at
the nginx layer, before traffic reaches your code. Requires the
http-auth plugin on the stack (install it with
`ownstack stack plugin-install http-auth`). `protect:status` reports
whether the plugin is installed, whether auth is enabled, the
configured users, and any IP/CIDR ranges allowed to bypass the prompt.
Add more users with `protect:add-user` and let trusted networks skip
the prompt with `protect:allow-ip`.

#### `app nuke`

Reset an app's Dokku-side state (apps:destroy + linked services) without touching the control-plane app, domains, env vars, or group.

Flags:
- `--stack=NAME_OR_ID` — Limit the nuke to a single stack instead of every stack the app deploys to.
- `--yes` — Skip the interactive name-match confirmation.

Examples:
```
ownstack app nuke <APP>    # Interactive — prompts you to retype the name to confirm.
ownstack app nuke <APP> --yes    # Non-interactive.
ownstack app nuke <APP> --stack=<STACK>    # Only nuke state on one stack (use when an app is on multiple stacks).
```

Notes: Use this when a Dokku build is stuck in a half-built state
(`Removing invalid image tag dokku/<app>:latest` with zero
buildpack output between cleanup and failure). Server-side
`AppNukeWorker` SSHs into each stack and runs `apps:destroy --force`
plus `postgres/redis/etc.:destroy` on linked services. The next
deploy rebuilds from scratch.

#### `app clone`

Clone an app — independent copy with its own database.

Flags:
- `--stack=NAME` — Target stack.
- `--domain=DOMAIN` — Custom domain TLD.
- `--letsencrypt-email=EMAIL`
- `--description=DESC`
- `--deploy` — Trigger deploy after creation.

Examples:
```
ownstack app clone <SOURCE> <NEW_NAME> [opts]
```

#### `app replicate`

Replicate an app — shares its database and Redis.

Flags:
- `--stack=NAME`
- `--domain=DOMAIN`
- `--letsencrypt-email=EMAIL`
- `--description=DESC`
- `--deploy`

Examples:
```
ownstack app replicate <SOURCE> <NEW_NAME> [opts]
```

#### `ssl-enable`

Enable Let's Encrypt for the linked app.

Flags:
- `--email=EMAIL` — Let's Encrypt account email.

Examples:
```
ownstack ssl-enable
ownstack ssl-enable --email=admin@example.com
```

#### `app group`

Show or set the AppGroup an app belongs to.

Flags:
- `--clear` — Remove the app from any group (sets app_group_id to null).

Examples:
```
ownstack app group    # Show the linked app's current group.
ownstack app group <APP>    # Show the named app's current group.
ownstack app group <APP> "Streamlit Apps"    # Assign by case-insensitive group name.
ownstack app group <APP> 18    # Assign by numeric group id.
ownstack app group <APP> --clear    # Remove from any group.
```

Notes: AppGroups are the sidebar groupings you see in the dashboard. Each app can belong
to one group (or none). The group is resolved by case-insensitive name or numeric id
within the current account. With no arguments, the app must be linked or passed
explicitly, and the current group is printed.

#### `app groups`

List app groups in the active account (id, name, app count, parent).

Examples:
```
ownstack app groups
```

#### `app domains` (aliases: app domains:list)

List the custom domains mapped to an app (id, domain, primary, SSL).

Examples:
```
ownstack app domains <APP>
ownstack app domains    # Uses the linked app in the current directory.
```

Notes: APP is optional when the current directory is linked to an app. The
SSL column shows "yes" when a stored certificate is attached to the
domain, otherwise a dash.

#### `app domains:add`

Map a custom domain to an app, optionally attaching an SSL cert and key.

Flags:
- `--cert=FILE` — Path to a certificate PEM file (use with --key).
- `--key=FILE` — Path to the matching private key PEM file (use with --cert).

Examples:
```
ownstack app domains:add <APP> app.example.com
ownstack app domains:add <APP> app.example.com --cert=fullchain.pem --key=privkey.pem    # Attach an explicit certificate and key.
```

Notes: Pass just the domain to use the linked app, or "APP domain" to target
a named app. With no cert, the control plane tries to auto-match a
stored certificate for the hostname. Provide --cert and --key together
to upload a specific certificate PEM and private key.

#### `app domains:remove`

Remove a mapped domain from an app by its domain id.

Examples:
```
ownstack app domains:remove <APP> <DOMAIN_ID>
ownstack app domains:remove <DOMAIN_ID>    # Remove from the linked app.
```

Notes: Run 'ownstack app domains [APP]' first to find the numeric domain id.
A single numeric argument is treated as the domain id on the linked app.

#### `app add-ons`

List, add, and remove an app's add-ons (Raven, Log Drain).

Flags:
- `--json` — Emit the add-on list as JSON.
- `--yes` — Skip the confirmation on remove.

Examples:
```
ownstack app add-ons <APP>    # Show each add-on as enabled / available / not configured.
ownstack app add-ons add my-app raven    # Enable Raven email for my-app. Sets RAVEN_API_KEY, RAVEN_BASE_URL and RAVEN_FROM and prints the sender.
ownstack app add-ons add <APP> logdrain    # Start shipping the app's logs to Log Drain (provisions in the background).
ownstack app add-ons remove my-app raven --yes    # Revoke the app's Raven keys and remove its RAVEN_* vars.
```

#### `app stop`

Stop all process types of an app on its stacks via the control plane (no SSH).

Flags:
- `--stack=NAME_OR_ID` — Act on a single stack instead of every stack the app deploys to.

Examples:
```
ownstack app stop <APP>
ownstack app stop <APP> --stack=<STACK>
```

Notes: Halts web and worker processes. Use before a destructive operation
such as a restore or schema change. Acts on every deployable stack
unless you narrow it with --stack.

#### `app start`

Start all process types of an app on its stacks via the control plane.

Flags:
- `--stack=NAME_OR_ID` — Act on a single stack instead of every stack the app deploys to.

Examples:
```
ownstack app start <APP>
ownstack app start <APP> --stack=<STACK>
```

#### `app restart`

Restart all process types of an app on its stacks via the control plane.

Flags:
- `--stack=NAME_OR_ID` — Act on a single stack instead of every stack the app deploys to.

Examples:
```
ownstack app restart <APP>
ownstack app restart <APP> --stack=<STACK>
```

#### `app processes` (aliases: app ps)

Show running process types and their scale per stack.

Examples:
```
ownstack app processes <APP>
ownstack app ps <APP>
```

#### `app scale`

Set how many containers run for one or more process types.

Flags:
- `--stack=NAME_OR_ID` — Scale only on this stack (default is every stack the app deploys to).

Examples:
```
ownstack app scale <APP> worker=1    # Run one worker container on every stack.
ownstack app scale <APP> web=2 worker=0 --stack=<STACK>    # Two web containers and no workers on one stack.
```

Notes: Pass one or more TYPE=COUNT pairs (e.g. worker=1 web=2). The type must
match a Procfile process type (lowercase letters, digits, - and _,
starting with a letter) and the count must be a non-negative integer;
0 stops that process type. The control plane saves the scale so it is
re-applied after every deploy, then runs dokku ps:scale on each of the
app's stacks now. Use --stack to change only one stack. Check the
result with `ownstack app ps <APP>`.

#### `app build-type`

Show or set an app's Dokku build type (dockerfile or herokuish buildpacks).

Examples:
```
ownstack app build-type <APP>    # Show the current build type.
ownstack app build-type <APP> dockerfile    # Build from the app's Dockerfile.
ownstack app build-type <APP> herokuish    # Build with Heroku buildpacks.
```

Notes: With no build type argument, prints the current setting. Pass
"dockerfile" or "herokuish" to change it. The change takes effect on
the next deploy.

#### `app limit` (aliases: app limits)

Show or set per-process-type memory limits (Dokku resource limits).

Flags:
- `--process-type=TYPE` — Process type to set or clear (e.g. web, worker).
- `--memory=SIZE` — Memory cap to set (e.g. 512m, 2g).
- `--clear` — Remove the limit on the given process type.
- `--restart` — Restart the process type after changing its limit.

Examples:
```
ownstack app limit <APP>    # List current limits.
ownstack app limit <APP> --process-type=worker --memory=2g --restart    # Cap the worker at 2g and restart it.
ownstack app limit <APP> --process-type=worker --clear    # Remove the worker limit.
```

Notes: With no flags, lists the current per-process limits (memory and CPU).
Pass --process-type with --memory to set a cap, or with --clear to
remove one. Add --restart to bounce the affected process afterward.

#### `app nginx`

Manage per-app nginx settings (upload limit, proxy timeouts) that survive a stack migration or clone.

Flags:
- `--no-push` — With set, save the value without applying it to the stacks yet.

Examples:
```
ownstack app nginx <APP>    # Show saved and live nginx settings.
ownstack app nginx set <APP> client-max-body-size 200m    # Raise the upload limit to 200MB and apply it now.
ownstack app nginx capture <APP>    # Import the app's current live overrides into the control plane (e.g. before a migration).
ownstack app nginx delete <APP> client-max-body-size    # Remove the saved upload-limit override.
ownstack app nginx push <APP>    # Replay saved settings onto the app's stacks.
```

Notes: The control plane persists these per-app nginx properties so they are
replayed onto any stack the app deploys to, instead of reverting to
Dokku defaults after a migration or clone (the fix for the 1MB
upload-cap regression). Subcommands:
  list (default)  show saved settings, the live values on the stack, and the supported keys
  set KEY VALUE   save a setting and (unless --no-push) apply it to the app's stacks now
  delete KEY      remove a saved setting and clear it on the stacks
  capture         import the live app's non-default overrides into the control plane
  push            replay all saved settings onto the app's stacks
Keys: client-max-body-size (e.g. 200m, 2g), proxy-read-timeout,
proxy-connect-timeout, proxy-send-timeout, keepalive-timeout, hsts-max-age.

#### `app repair-db`

Re-link an app's Postgres or MySQL service on its stack when DATABASE_URL drifted from the linked service.

Flags:
- `--stack=NAME_OR_ID` — Stack to repair on. Defaults to the app's primary stack.
- `--check-only` — Report what would change without repairing the link.

Examples:
```
ownstack app repair-db postgres <APP>    # Re-link the app's Postgres service on its primary stack.
ownstack app repair-db mysql <APP> --stack=<STACK>    # Re-link MySQL on a specific stack.
ownstack app repair-db postgres <APP> --check-only    # Dry run, no changes.
```

Notes: Server-side the control plane re-runs the Dokku link so DATABASE_URL
(or the MySQL DSN) points at the app's own service again. ENGINE is
required and must be postgres or mysql. APP defaults to the linked app;
the stack defaults to the app's primary stack.

#### `app purge-cache`

Clear the Dokku build cache and stale docker image for an app on each of its stacks (SSH).

Examples:
```
ownstack app purge-cache <APP>
ownstack app purge-cache    # Uses the linked app in the current directory.
```

Notes: SSHes into every stack the app deploys to and runs
`repo:purge-cache` plus a docker image purge, forcing the next deploy
to rebuild from a clean cache. APP defaults to the linked app.

#### `app unlock`

Release a stale Dokku deploy lock for an app on each of its stacks (SSH).

Examples:
```
ownstack app unlock <APP>
ownstack app unlock    # Uses the linked app in the current directory.
```

Notes: SSHes into each stack and runs `apps:unlock`. Use this when a prior
deploy was interrupted and left a lock behind that blocks new deploys.
Unlock does not stop a deploy that is genuinely still running. APP
defaults to the linked app.

#### `app data heroku`

Snapshot and download a Heroku app's database into an OwnStack stack.

Flags:
- `--heroku-app=NAME` — For start. The Heroku app to snapshot.
- `--stack=NAME` — For start. The OwnStack stack that receives the download.

Examples:
```
ownstack app data heroku list <APP>
ownstack app data heroku apps <APP>
ownstack app data heroku start <APP> --heroku-app=my-heroku --stack=<STACK>
ownstack app data heroku delete <APP> <IMPORT_ID>
```

Notes: Subcommands (APP defaults to the linked app):
list [APP] shows past Heroku data imports; apps [APP] lists the Heroku
apps you can pull from (with Postgres and MySQL flags); start [APP]
creates a snapshot and download; delete [APP] IMPORT_ID removes a
download.

#### `app data import`

Inspect and run a database import into an app from a prepared dump.

Flags:
- `--tables=LIST` — For execute. Comma-separated table:mode pairs, e.g. users:replace,orders:amend.

Examples:
```
ownstack app data import list <APP>
ownstack app data import status <APP> <IMPORT_ID>
ownstack app data import tables <APP> <IMPORT_ID>
ownstack app data import execute <APP> <IMPORT_ID> --tables=users:replace,orders:amend
```

Notes: Subcommands (APP defaults to the linked app):
list [APP] shows database imports; status [APP] IMPORT_ID shows an
import's status and tables; tables [APP] IMPORT_ID refreshes the table
list from the dump; execute [APP] IMPORT_ID applies selected tables.
Each table takes a mode of replace (truncate then insert) or amend
(append).

### SSL certificates

Certificates live in an account-scoped "locker" (`/api/ssl_certificates`).
Each cert can be pushed to one or more apps; pushing writes the cert into
Dokku's per-app `tls/` directory and rebuilds nginx with a `listen 443 ssl`
block. Pushes are asynchronous — the CLI enqueues a `SslCertificatePushWorker`
job and polls for the result before reporting success/fail per stack.

DNS for Let's Encrypt (DNS-01): domains whose zones live in OwnStack's
platform Hetzner Cloud DNS need nothing connected. The control plane
writes the challenge records to Hetzner itself, for issuance and for
auto-renewal. For a domain hosted in your own AWS account, connect
Route53 (`ownstack route53 connect`). DNSimple is a legacy, optional
integration (`ownstack dnsimple`), kept for zones still hosted there;
it is not required for anything. To issue a cert locally, `sslgen`
defaults to Hetzner Cloud DNS (token from `HCLOUD_TOKEN` or the hcloud
CLI config), with `--dns route53` and `--manual-dns` as alternatives.

#### `cert publish`

Upload a sslgen cert (fullchain.pem + privkey.pem) to the locker, then push to an app.

Flags:
- `--app=APP` — App name or id to push the cert to. Required.
- `--cert-dir=DIR` — Directory containing fullchain.pem and privkey.pem. Defaults to ~/.sslgen/certs/ownstack.org.
- `--name=NAME` — Display name for the locker entry. Defaults to basename of --cert-dir.
- `--stack=NAME` — Push only to the given stack instead of every stack the app deploys to.

Examples:
```
sslgen request example.com    # Issue a wildcard cert (example.com + *.example.com) using Hetzner Cloud DNS.
ownstack cert publish --app my-app --cert-dir ~/.sslgen/certs/example.com
```

Notes: Each invocation uploads a new locker entry. To attach the same cert
to multiple apps without duplicates, run `cert publish` once and then
`cert push --cert-id=N --app=APP` for each additional app.

Issue the cert first with sslgen, which answers the DNS-01 challenge
on Hetzner Cloud DNS by default:
`sslgen request example.com` (writes ~/.sslgen/certs/example.com).
Test with `--staging` first; use `--dns route53 --aws-profile NAME`
for a Route53 zone, or `--manual-dns` for anything else.

#### `cert list` (aliases: cert ls)

List certificates in the locker (id, name, not-after).

Examples:
```
ownstack cert list
```

#### `cert push`

Push an existing locker certificate to an app — no re-upload, no duplicate locker entries.

Flags:
- `--cert-id=N` — Locker certificate id (from `ownstack cert list`). Required.
- `--app=APP` — App name or id. Required.
- `--stack=NAME_OR_ID` — Push to one stack instead of every deployable stack on the app.

Examples:
```
ownstack cert list    # Find the cert id you want to reuse.
ownstack cert push --cert-id=12 --app=my-other-app    # Attach an existing cert to another app.
```

Notes: Use this when you already uploaded a wildcard cert (e.g., for
*.apps.example.com) and just want to attach it to a new app.

#### `cert renew`

Re-issue a locker certificate via Let's Encrypt and re-push it to every app using it.

Flags:
- `--cert-id=N` — Locker certificate id (from `ownstack cert list`).
- `--expiring` — Instead of one cert, renew every locker cert expiring within the account's renewal window (the on-demand version of the daily sweep; works with auto-renew off).

Examples:
```
ownstack cert list    # Find the expiring cert id.
ownstack cert renew --cert-id=12    # Re-issue and re-push in one shot.
ownstack cert renew --expiring    # Renew everything inside the renewal window now.
```

Notes: The control plane answers the DNS-01 challenge with TXT records on
whichever DNS provider holds the cert's domains: platform Hetzner
Cloud DNS (automatic, nothing to connect) for domains in OwnStack's
Hetzner zones, otherwise a connected Route53 integration
(`ownstack route53 connect`), or the legacy DNSimple integration if
one is connected. It then updates the locker entry in place and
re-pushes to all apps whose `ssl_certificate_id` references the cert.
Issuance takes a few minutes; the CLI polls until the job completes.
Certs expiring within 30 days renew automatically (when auto-renew is
on, for integrations). This command is for renewing on demand.

#### `dnsimple`

Manage the account's legacy DNSimple integration (optional; Let's Encrypt issuance and auto-renewal for zones hosted at DNSimple).

Flags:
- `--token=TOKEN` — For `connect` — the DNSimple account API token. Prompts on stdin if omitted (keeps the secret out of shell history).
- `--days=N` — For `auto-renew` — renew certs expiring within N days (1-89, default 30). Combinable with on|off.

Examples:
```
ownstack dnsimple status    # Show connection and auto-renew state.
ownstack dnsimple connect    # Link a DNSimple account token (prompted).
ownstack dnsimple auto-renew off    # Pause automatic renewals; `on` re-enables.
ownstack dnsimple auto-renew --days=45    # Widen the renewal window to 45 days before expiry.
ownstack dnsimple disconnect    # Remove the integration.
```

Notes: Legacy and optional. OwnStack's own DNS runs on Hetzner Cloud DNS,
which the control plane uses automatically, and Route53
(`ownstack route53`) is the documented integration for zones in your
own AWS account. Connect DNSimple only for zones still hosted there.

One DNSimple connection per account. The token must be a DNSimple
*account* token (DNSimple → Account → Automation → API tokens); user
tokens are rejected because they carry no account identity. With
auto-renew on (the default), a daily job re-issues any locker cert
expiring within 30 days whose domains are hosted in the connected
DNSimple account, then re-pushes it to the apps using it. Same
integration as Settings → Integrations → DNSimple in the dashboard.

#### `route53`

Manage the account's Route53 integration (powers Let's Encrypt issuance and auto-renewal).

Flags:
- `--credential=NAME_OR_ID` — For `connect` — reuse a saved AWS credential from the account's credential vault instead of pasting a key pair.
- `--access-key-id=AKIA...` — For `connect` — the AWS access key id (when not using --credential).
- `--secret-access-key=KEY` — For `connect` — the AWS secret. Prompts on stdin if omitted (keeps the secret out of shell history).
- `--region=REGION` — For `connect` — AWS region for the client (Route53 is global; default us-east-1).
- `--days=N` — For `auto-renew` — renew certs expiring within N days (1-89, default 30). Combinable with on|off.

Examples:
```
ownstack route53 status    # Show connection and auto-renew state.
ownstack route53 connect --credential=prod-aws    # Link using a saved AWS credential.
ownstack route53 connect --access-key-id=AKIA123EXAMPLE    # Link a raw key pair (secret prompted).
ownstack route53 auto-renew off    # Pause automatic renewals; `on` re-enables.
```
